title: Freelance Past Client Win-Back Kit
description: Fill a quiet month with work from people who already hired you. Build and score a list of past clients, find a real reason to contact each one, adapt ten short message templates plus follow-ups, run a ten-day plan at 20-40 minutes a day, and handle every kind of reply. Includes a worked example, a scored client list and an outreach log.

files.01-build-your-list.md:
# Build Your Win-Back List

Most freelancers underestimate how many past clients they have and how few of them they've stayed in touch with. This step gets everyone into one place and tells you who to contact first.

## Step 1: gather every past client

Go through these sources and add a row to `past-clients.csv` for each client from the last three years:

- Invoices and your accounting or invoicing tool
- Sent proposals (including ones that went quiet but where you did a small job)
- Email folders and project folders
- Old contracts
- Your portfolio and case studies
- Messaging apps and platform inboxes

Include small one-off jobs. A $200 job three years ago can still be a $3,000 job today.

Also include the person, not just the company. If your contact moved to a new company, that's two leads: the old company and the new one.

## Step 2: fill in the facts

For each row, fill in:

| Column | What to write |
|---|---|
| `client` / `contact_name` / `contact_role` | Who you worked with |
| `last_project` | One short phrase |
| `last_project_end` | Month and year is enough |
| `total_billed` | Approximate is fine |
| `how_it_ended` | `great`, `fine` or `rocky` |
| `still_there` | Is the contact still at that company? Check their public profile if unsure. `yes`, `moved` or `unknown` |

## Step 3: score each one

Give each client 1-3 points in four columns:

| Column | 1 | 2 | 3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Relationship** | Rocky or distant | Fine, professional | They liked working with you and said so |
| **Fit** | Work you don't want to do again | OK work | Exactly the work you want more of |
| **Recency** | Over 2 years ago | 1-2 years ago | Within the last year |
| **Likely need** | No obvious reason they'd need you now | Possible need | A clear reason: growth, launch, seasonal cycle, the work you did needs updating |

**Priority = Relationship + Fit + Recency + (Likely need x 2)**

Likely need counts double because a reason to get in touch is what makes the message land. Maximum is 15.

## Step 4: sort into three groups

| Group | Score | What you'll do |
|---|---|---|
| **A: Contact this week** | 11-15 | A personal message with a specific idea or reason |
| **B: Contact next** | 7-10 | A personal message with a lighter reason, or a useful share |
| **C: Keep warm** | 4-6 | Add to your quarterly check-in list; no push now |

Remove anyone where it ended badly and you wouldn't want to work with them again. That's not a lead; it's a risk.

## Step 5: find a reason for each A and B client

Spend two minutes per A and B client looking for a reason to write. Note it in the `reason_to_contact` column. Places to look:

- **Their website and social posts.** New product, new hire, new location, rebrand, a page that's clearly out of date.
- **Your own past work for them.** Is it due for an update? Did you notice something you'd improve now?
- **The calendar.** Year-end, budgets, a seasonal busy period, an anniversary of the project.
- **Your business.** A new service, a new skill, a package that fits what they used to ask for.
- **Something useful.** An article, a tool, a contact you could introduce them to.

If you can't find any reason for an A client, drop them to B.

## Step 6: choose the template

In the `template` column, pick the template from `02-message-templates.md` that fits the reason. You're now ready for the ten-day plan.

## What a good list looks like

For a freelancer with three years of work, a typical list might be 20-40 clients, with around 5-10 in group A. If your list is shorter, that's fine. Win-back works with small numbers because each message is personal.
files.02-message-templates.md:
# Message Templates

Ten short messages for different reasons to get back in touch, plus follow-ups. They work as email, LinkedIn messages or whatever channel you used with the client.

## Before you send any of these

- **Rewrite the first line every time.** It should only make sense for this one person. Templates are the skeleton; the first line is what gets a reply.
- **Keep it under 120 words.** Past clients know you. You don't need to re-introduce yourself.
- **End with one easy question.** Something they can answer in a few words.
- **Send from your normal address, one at a time.** Not a mail-merge blast with tracking pixels.

Square brackets are things to replace.

---

## T1: Your past work needs an update

**When:** Something you made for them is now out of date (old dates, old prices, old team, old branding, broken links).

> Subject: Your [project] from [year]
>
> Hi [name],
>
> I was looking back at the [project] we did together and noticed [specific thing: the pricing page still shows last year's rates / the team page is missing your two new hires]. Easy to let slide when you're busy.
>
> If it'd help, I could update it [scope: the three pages that changed] for [price or "a small fixed fee"] and have it done by [date].
>
> Worth doing?
>
> [Your name]

## T2: A specific idea

**When:** You've noticed something in their business (new launch, new location, new market) and have a concrete idea.

> Subject: Idea for [their new thing]
>
> Hi [name],
>
> Congratulations on [specific news]. [One genuine sentence about it.]
>
> It made me think: [one specific idea, one or two sentences, framed around their benefit]. I did something similar for [type of client, no names unless you have permission] and [real, modest result or what it involved].
>
> Would it be useful if I sketched out what that could look like for you? No charge for the outline.
>
> [Your name]

## T3: New service that fits them

**When:** You now offer something you didn't when you last worked together, and it fits what they used to ask about.

> Subject: Something you asked about in [year]
>
> Hi [name],
>
> When we worked on [project], you mentioned [thing they wanted / problem they had]. At the time it wasn't something I offered.
>
> I do now: [one-line description of the service, price if it's a package]. Given [their situation], I thought of you first.
>
> Is that still on your list, or has it been sorted?
>
> [Your name]

## T4: Open spot

**When:** You have a gap and they're a good-fit client who's likely to have work. Use sparingly and only with A clients.

> Subject: Opening in [month]
>
> Hi [name],
>
> I've got space for one project starting [date], and you were one of the first people I wanted to tell. I really enjoyed working on [project].
>
> If there's anything on your list, [type of work you'd like to do for them, e.g. "the product pages you mentioned"], I'd be glad to take it on.
>
> Anything coming up?
>
> [Your name]

Don't apologise for being available and don't offer a discount here. "First people I wanted to tell" is the value.

## T5: They moved companies

**When:** Your contact has a new role elsewhere.

> Subject: Congratulations on [new company]
>
> Hi [name],
>
> I saw you've moved to [new company] as [role]. Congratulations, that's a great fit.
>
> New roles often come with a list of things to fix. If [type of work you do] is on yours, I'd be glad to help, the same way we worked on [past project].
>
> Either way, good luck in the new job.
>
> [Your name]

Also consider sending T7 or T1 to whoever replaced them at the old company.

## T6: Useful share, no ask

**When:** Group B clients, or anyone you want to warm up before asking. Only send things that are genuinely useful to them.

> Subject: Thought of you: [topic]
>
> Hi [name],
>
> I came across [article / tool / contact / change in a rule that affects their industry] and thought of you because [specific reason tied to their business].
>
> [One-sentence summary of why it matters.] [Link or details.]
>
> Hope [something specific: the new shop / the busy season] is going well.
>
> [Your name]

No ask is the point. Replies to these often turn into a conversation about work anyway.

## T7: New contact at an old client

**When:** Your old contact left and someone new is in the role.

> Subject: [Company]'s [project] from [year]
>
> Hi [new name],
>
> I worked with [old contact] on [project] for [company] in [year]. I gather you've taken over [their area]. Congratulations.
>
> I know the background of [project], so if anything needs updating or extending, I can get going quickly without a long briefing. I've attached / linked [the original files or a short summary] in case it's useful to have.
>
> Happy to have a quick call if that would help you get up to speed.
>
> [Your name]

## T8: Seasonal or calendar reason

**When:** A predictable cycle: year-end, budgets, a busy season, a yearly event, an anniversary of the project.

> Subject: Before [season / event]
>
> Hi [name],
>
> Last year we [did X] ahead of [season/event]. With [season/event] coming up again on [date], I wanted to check whether you're planning anything similar this year.
>
> If so, booking by [date] would give us comfortable time to [deliver / test / print].
>
> Shall I hold a spot?
>
> [Your name]

## T9: Honest check-in

**When:** You have no specific reason, the relationship is good, and it's been over six months. This is the fallback, not the default.

> Subject: How's [specific thing] going?
>
> Hi [name],
>
> It's been a while since [project], and I was wondering how [specific thing: the launch / the new site / the team] has gone.
>
> I'm currently booking work for [month] and would be glad to help if anything's come up. And if not, I'd still like to hear how things are.
>
> [Your name]

## T10: Referral ask

**When:** Great relationship, but they're unlikely to need you themselves right now.

> Subject: Quick question
>
> Hi [name],
>
> I hope [specific] is going well.
>
> I'm looking for one or two more [type of client] to work with in [month]. You know how I work better than most, so I wanted to ask: is there anyone you know who's dealing with [specific problem you solve]?
>
> No pressure at all. If someone comes to mind, I'm happy for you to share my email.
>
> [Your name]

---

## Follow-ups

Send one follow-up after 6-8 working days if there's no reply. Reply in the same thread so they can see the original.

**Follow-up A (short nudge):**
> Hi [name], just bringing this back to the top of your inbox in case it got buried. [Repeat the one question in a few words.]

**Follow-up B (add something):**
> Hi [name], one more thought on this: [a small extra detail, example or idea]. Happy to leave it if the timing isn't right.

**Follow-up C (easy no):**
> Hi [name], I'll take silence as "not right now", which is completely fine. I'll check back in [season]. Good luck with [specific].

After one follow-up, stop. Move them to your quarterly list and note the date in `outreach-log.csv`.

## Subject lines that work

Short, specific and boring wins. Their name for the project, the name of their new thing, or a plain question.

Avoid: "Quick favour", "Exciting news!", "Are you still interested?", anything in capitals, and fake "Re:" or "Fwd:" prefixes.
files.03-ten-day-plan.md:
# Ten-Day Win-Back Plan

A focused push for a quiet stretch. Ten working days, 20-40 minutes a day, alongside whatever other work you have. The aim is not to message everyone at once; it's to send a few good messages a day and handle replies quickly.

## Before Day 1

- [ ] `past-clients.csv` filled in, scored and grouped (see `01-build-your-list.md`)
- [ ] A reason noted for each A and B client
- [ ] Decide what you'll offer: which services, which start dates, any package with a fixed price
- [ ] Block 30 minutes in your calendar for each of the next ten working days
- [ ] Open `outreach-log.csv`

## The plan

| Day | Main task | Messages to send | Also |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Top three A clients | 3 personal messages (T1, T2 or T3 work best) | Log each one |
| 2 | Next three A clients | 3 | Reply to anything that came in within a few hours |
| 3 | Remaining A clients | 2-4 | Check your portfolio link and package page work |
| 4 | First B clients | 3 (T6 useful share is good here) | |
| 5 | Moved contacts | T5 to anyone who changed jobs, T7 to their replacements | Midpoint check (below) |
| 6 | More B clients | 3 | |
| 7 | Referral asks | T10 to 2-3 happy clients unlikely to need you now | |
| 8 | Follow-ups | Follow up Day 1-2 messages with no reply | |
| 9 | Follow-ups | Follow up Day 3-4 messages with no reply | |
| 10 | Review and set up | Follow up Day 5-6 messages; review results (below) | Set quarterly reminders |

Days 8-10 are lighter on new messages on purpose. Replies and follow-ups are where projects get booked.

## Daily routine (20-40 minutes)

1. **Check replies first** (5 min). Answer within the same working day using `04-handling-replies.md`.
2. **Look up the next people** (2-3 min each). Recheck their website or posts for anything new since you built the list.
3. **Write and send** (5 min each). Rewrite the first line. Read it out loud once before sending.
4. **Log** (2 min). One row per message in `outreach-log.csv`.

## Midpoint check (Day 5)

Look at your log:

| What you see | What to do |
|---|---|
| Replies to more than a third of messages | Keep going as planned |
| A few replies, all "not now" | Normal. Note their timing and set a reminder for it |
| No replies at all after 10+ messages | Reread three messages. Are the first lines specific? Is the ask easy to answer? Is it under 120 words? Rewrite and try T2 or T1, which tend to work best |
| Replies but no projects | Make your offer more concrete: a package, a price, a start date |

## Day 10 review

Count:

- Messages sent: ____
- Replies: ____
- Conversations or calls: ____
- Proposals or quotes sent: ____
- Projects booked: ____ worth $____
- Referrals received: ____
- "Not now, try in [month]": ____

Then note which templates got replies. Use those first next time.

## Stay in touch after this (so you don't need another push)

Set these recurring reminders now:

| How often | What | Who |
|---|---|---|
| Every 3 months | One personal message with a reason (T1, T2, T6 or T8) | Group A clients |
| Every 6 months | One useful share or check-in | Group B clients |
| Once a year | One check-in | Group C clients |
| When a "not now" named a month | Message on that month | Anyone who gave timing |

Fifteen minutes a week, two or three messages, is usually enough to keep a past-client list warm.
files.04-handling-replies.md:
# Handling Replies

A reply is where the work gets booked, or lost. Answer within the same working day if you can, keep it short, and always move to one clear next step.

## "Yes, actually, we need [thing]"

Move fast and make the next step concrete.

> Great to hear from you. [Thing] sounds very doable. To give you an accurate price and timeline, I'd like to ask a few questions. Would a 20-minute call on [two specific times] work? Or if you prefer, I can send three quick questions by email.

Then:

- If it fits a package you offer, send the package details and the next start date.
- If it's custom, run your normal quote or proposal process.
- Don't drop your price because they're a past client. Your rate today is your rate today. If your price has gone up since you last worked together, say so plainly: "My rates have changed since [year]; this would be [price]."

## "Maybe, tell me more"

They're interested but not sold. Give them one concrete thing to react to.

> Happy to. For [their situation], I'd suggest [specific scope in one or two sentences]. That would be around [price or range] and take about [time]. Does that sound roughly like what you had in mind, or would something smaller be a better start?

Offering a smaller first step often turns a maybe into a yes.

## "Not right now, but maybe in [month]"

This is a good reply. It's a date.

> Thanks, that's really helpful. I'll check back in [month]. If anything changes before then, you know where I am.

Then:

- Add the month to `outreach-log.csv` in `next_action_date`.
- Set a calendar reminder.
- When the month comes, open with: "You mentioned [month] might be a good time to look at [thing]..."

## "No, we're all set"

Thank them and leave the door open. One line, no pushback.

> Totally understood, thanks for letting me know. Good luck with [specific], and feel free to get in touch any time.

Move them to group C. Consider a T10 referral ask in a few months if the relationship was good.

## "We've hired someone else / brought it in-house"

> Thanks for telling me, and congratulations on growing the team. If they ever need an extra pair of hands for overflow or a specific project, I'm happy to help.

Overflow work from in-house teams is real work. Note it.

## "Can you do it cheaper?"

> I understand. The price reflects [what's included]. If budget is the main thing, I could do [smaller scope] for [lower price], which would cover [the most important part]. Would that work?

Reduce the scope, not the rate.

## "Who are you again?"

It happens. Don't be offended.

> Of course, it's been a while. I'm [name]; I [did project] for [company] in [year]. [One line on why you got in touch.]

## A referral comes back

> Thanks so much for thinking of me. I'll get in touch with [person] today and mention you introduced us.

Then:

- Contact the referred person the same day.
- Tell your past client how it went, whatever the outcome.
- Thank them properly if it turns into work (a handwritten note, a small gift or simply a sincere message; check whether their employer has rules about gifts).

## An awkward reply (unpaid invoice, old complaint)

If a past client raises something unresolved, deal with it before anything else:

> Thanks for raising that. I'd like to sort it out properly. [Your proposed fix or a request for a call.]

Don't pitch until it's resolved. Fixing an old issue well often rebuilds trust faster than any pitch.

## After any reply

- [ ] Logged in `outreach-log.csv` with the outcome
- [ ] Next action and date set
- [ ] Calendar reminder created if there's a future date
files.05-worked-example.md:
# Worked Example: Ten Days of Win-Back

A fictional freelance graphic designer, Ola, has a three-week gap starting next month. Everything here is invented to show the method; your numbers will be different.

## The list

Ola spends an hour pulling clients from three years of invoices and email. She finds 26 past clients and scores them.

| Group | Count | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| A (11-15) | 6 | A bakery opening a second shop; a former contact now at a new firm; a charity with an annual report due |
| B (7-10) | 11 | A yoga studio with a new season; a consultant whose website still shows an old logo |
| C (4-6) | 7 | One-off jobs from over two years ago |
| Removed | 2 | One rocky project; one client who paid very late twice |

## Days 1-3: the A clients

**Bakery (T2 specific idea).** She'd seen the post about the second shop.

> Subject: Idea for the new shop
>
> Hi Sam,
>
> Congratulations on the second shop. The photo of the counter looks great.
>
> It made me think: the menu and price boards we did in 2025 were sized for the original shop's wall. A version adapted to the new space would keep both shops looking like one brand from day one.
>
> Would it be useful if I sketched out what that would involve? No charge for the outline.
>
> Ola

Sam replied within two hours: "Yes please, we open in five weeks."

**Former contact at a new firm (T5).** Priya had moved to a mid-size accounting firm. Ola sent a T5 and, separately, a T7 to Priya's replacement at the old company.

**Charity annual report (T8 seasonal).** Last year's report was delivered in March. Ola wrote now, well ahead of the next one, offering to hold a spot.

Three more A messages went out on Day 3.

## Day 5: midpoint

| Sent | Replies | Calls booked | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 11 | 5 | 2 | Two "not now", one "who's this?" (answered politely) |

Over a third had replied, so she kept going without changes.

## Days 6-7: B clients and referrals

- T6 (useful share) to four B clients, including a note to the yoga studio about a change to local signage rules she'd read about, with a link to the official page.
- T10 referral asks to two happy clients who weren't likely to need design work this year.

One referral came back: a friend of the consultant needed a pitch deck redesigned.

## Days 8-10: follow-ups

She sent Follow-up A to five people who hadn't replied. Two replied: one "not until spring" (logged for April) and one small job for social media templates.

## Results after ten days

| Measure | Count |
|---|---|
| Messages sent (first contact) | 19 |
| Follow-ups | 5 |
| Replies | 10 |
| Calls | 4 |
| Quotes sent | 4 |
| Projects booked | 3 (bakery boards, social templates, referred pitch deck) |
| "Not now" with a date | 3 |
| Referrals | 1 |

The three-week gap was mostly filled, and three more conversations had dates attached for the following months.

## What Ola changed for next time

- T2 (specific idea) and T8 (seasonal) got the most replies. She'll lead with those.
- T9 (honest check-in) got no replies from three sends. She'll only use it when she really has nothing else.
- She set a quarterly 30-minute reminder to send three messages to group A clients, so the next gap is smaller or doesn't happen.
files.README.md:
# Freelance Past Client Win-Back Kit

Your easiest next project is often with someone who has already hired you, paid you and liked the result. This kit helps you get back in touch with past clients in a way that feels helpful rather than needy, and turn a quiet month into booked work.

## Who this is for

Freelancers with at least five past clients who:

- have a gap in the calendar coming up,
- haven't spoken to most past clients since the last invoice was paid, or
- feel awkward "just checking in" and so never do.

## What's inside

| File | What it does | Time |
|---|---|---|
| `01-build-your-list.md` | Pull every past client into one list and sort them into who to contact first | 45 min |
| `past-clients.csv` | The list itself, with scoring columns and three example rows | 30 min |
| `02-message-templates.md` | Ten short, ready-to-adapt messages for different situations, plus follow-ups | Reference |
| `03-ten-day-plan.md` | A day-by-day plan for a focused win-back push when work is quiet | 20-40 min a day |
| `04-handling-replies.md` | What to say when they reply: yes, maybe, not now, no, and referrals | Reference |
| `05-worked-example.md` | A fictional designer's ten days, from list to booked work, step by step | Read: 10 min |
| `outreach-log.csv` | Track who you contacted, when, what you sent and what happened | Ongoing |

## How to use it

1. Build and score your list (`01-build-your-list.md`, `past-clients.csv`).
2. Pick the right template for each person (`02-message-templates.md`). Personalise the first line every time.
3. Work through the `03-ten-day-plan.md`, logging everything in `outreach-log.csv`.
4. Use `04-handling-replies.md` the moment someone answers.
5. After the push, set the quarterly reminder at the end of the ten-day plan so you never go this long without contact again.

## Three rules that make this work

1. **Every message has a reason.** A specific idea, a relevant change, something you noticed. "Just checking in" is the last resort, not the first.
2. **One ask, easy to answer.** Yes/no questions or "worth a chat?" beat "let me know if you need anything".
3. **Follow up once, then stop.** One polite follow-up after about a week. After that, they go back to your quarterly list.

## Opening the files

- `.md` files open in any text editor or notes app.
- `.csv` files open in Excel, Google Sheets, Numbers or LibreOffice.

Only contact people you've worked with or who have agreed to hear from you, and follow the email and privacy rules that apply where you and they are based.
